demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
He is 28, a Latin American man who has been married for three years, and he works as a prison guard at a county facility on the edge of the city. When he talks about his life before the loss, he describes it in simple, steady terms. He works long shifts, comes home tired, eats late with his wife, and calls his younger brother whenever he has a few minutes between days. His brother is the person who makes him laugh fastest, the one who sends voice notes full of jokes and gossip from back home, the one who asks about married life and teases him for becoming serious. He says they have always stayed close, even after migration scattered the family.

The night his brother dies begins like an ordinary workday. He is on shift when his phone vibrates in his locker. He does not see the missed calls until his break. By then there are several messages from family, each one more urgent than the last. He calls back and learns that his brother has been in a car accident and is already gone. He remembers standing in the staff hallway staring at the cinderblock wall while another officer is talking to him, but he cannot understand the words. What he remembers clearly is the feeling that something in his body has dropped out from under him. He keeps saying, “No, no, no,” as if repetition might reverse time. Because he is at work, surrounded by locked doors and routine, he tries to keep himself together until he can leave. Later he feels ashamed that he finished paperwork before driving home, but at the time he is moving like a machine.

In the first weeks afterward, he sleeps very little. When he does sleep, he wakes with the sensation that the phone is ringing again, that he has missed the call and can still answer it if he moves fast enough. He replays the moment in the hallway over and over. He also imagines the crash in intrusive fragments, though he was never there to see it. A bent door, broken glass, his brother alone. He knows these images are constructed from fear and secondhand details, but they come anyway. His wife wakes to find him sitting on the edge of the bed at 3 a.m., elbows on knees, staring at the floor. Sometimes she touches his back and he flinches before he recognizes her.

Returning fully to work makes things worse in ways he does not expect. The noise of gates slamming and men shouting sends a jolt through him. Over the prison radio, sudden calls for backup make his heart pound so hard he feels briefly embarrassed, as if other officers can see it. He becomes more watchful on the unit, scanning faces, exits, hands. He tells himself this makes him a better guard, but he also knows it is exhausting. If an inmate starts yelling unexpectedly, his whole body tenses. At home he is no calmer. He checks locks twice. If his wife is late getting home, he calls repeatedly, then hates how desperate he sounds when she answers.

He avoids things that pull him toward his brother. For months he cannot listen to the music they used to play in the car. He lets family group messages pile up unread because he cannot bear photos or memorial posts. He skips a cousin’s birthday party after hearing there will be a slideshow. His wife urges him gently to visit his mother, but he keeps postponing the trip, saying work is too busy. The truth, he says, is that he cannot tolerate the idea of entering his mother’s house and feeling his brother missing from it.

He has changed in the marriage too. Before, he describes himself as affectionate, joking, easy to talk to. Now his wife tells him he is physically present but far away. He comes home from a shift and sits in silence at the kitchen table, still in uniform, scrolling through old messages from his brother without opening them. Small disagreements turn sharp quickly. If she asks whether he is okay, he sometimes snaps, “I’m fine,” in a tone that ends the conversation. A few minutes later he feels guilty and goes quiet again. He says the guilt sits on top of another guilt he cannot shake: that he was checking inmate counts and filling out reports while his brother was dying.

He notices that the world feels less safe and less predictable than it once did. At work he sees young men acting invincible and feels sudden anger at them, though he knows it does not make sense. On the drive home he is tense around intersections, watching other cars too closely. He has started taking longer routes if traffic is heavy. Some nights he pours a drink to relax, then another, though he insists he is trying not to make that a habit.

In session, when he speaks about his brother directly, his voice becomes softer, almost boyish. He remembers how his brother laughed with his whole body, how he would call just to say he had seen something stupid and thought of him. He says the hardest part is that life has continued with such disrespectful normality. He still clocks in, checks doors, writes reports, buys groceries, pays bills. Yet part of him remains in that hallway at work, staring at his phone, caught in the moment before and after everything changed.
